As a result of this suggestion we obtained large steel draggers, went out in the bay of Fundy and caught a great deal of fish, but by the time we sold them, considering that they had to be processed, we only had about 30 per cent left. The fish are gutted at sea and the livers and everything is thrown away, and all we have left are the clippings. I do not think the large monopolies are making any money in this industry, but rather that the small operator is making money. When we were small and used the small draggers in the bay of Fundy we were making money. I think in respect of every pound of fish we sell this year we will lose money.

That is the Liberal government for you.
Supply-Fisheries
I assure you that we are losing money.
I do not believe you.

You should have a look at our balance sheets if you do not believe me. You do not know anything about the fishing business or you would not question my statement, but would pat me on the back and state that I am right.
I have nothing more to say, Mr. Chairman, except to repeat that more research should be done in respect of this industry.
When a producer buys a fish in the raw he may pay five cents per pound for it, but when you buy the same type of fish at the market it likely will cost 40 cents per pound. To understand this situation you must realize that only 30 per cent of the raw fish is marketable. People are inclined to suggest that the monopolies are making a great deal of money because they have to pay 40 cents a pound for fish at the market. They should keep in mind that the same fish is sold in the raw for perhaps four or five cents a pound. I bring this information to your attention so that when you go to the store and have to pay that much for fish you will not complain because you will be aware of the situation, and realize that the fisherman is not making a lot of money.
At this time there is a very serious scarcity of fish and I do not believe the processors are going to make any money this year. We must have more research in respect of the sardine industry. You might suggest that this is a very lowly industry, but I point out that it amounts to $6 million in my county alone, and the products are sold all over the world. One can go to any foreign country in the world and mention the word "sardine" and the people there will understand what you are talking about, whereas you may mention wheat, or any of a variety of foodstuffs or products and the people are just as likely not to know what you mean. I repeat that we must have more research in respect of this industry, not that it will mean anything to me personally, but it will mean a great deal to a future generation in my county in the province of New Brunswick. I suggest that the fisheries department should pay more attention to this particular fishery.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Charlotte who has given us some information about this very important sardine industry, and has referred to the need for research in respect of the

Supply-Fisheries
mysteries of that particular fish. As the hon. member was speaking I thought that he was at least in a more fortunate situation than I, in that one of the fishing industries in British Columbia has completely disappeared. The sardine, whether large or small, is still in existence, but one of the unsolved mysteries on the west coast is the complete disappearance of the pilchard. The pilchard used to swarm in very large numbers, but to my knowledge no one has seen even one for a number of years.
I am very pleased that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is in his seat tonight to listen to the discussion we are having in respect of the Department of Fisheries. I am sure he was interested earlier in the evening when my colleague from Skeena was talking about the oolachan, which is of importance to many of the native Indian people on the west coast. In view of the situation the hon. member for Skeena described as existing at the mouth of the Kitimat river, I think perhaps I should explain that the oolachan which he presented to the Minister of Fisheries came from the Nass. I suggest the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in his capacity as superintendent general of Indian affairs, should not lose an early opportunity of sampling these small oolachan, a sample of which I am sure the hon. member for Skeena would be pleased to provide.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about a matter in which I think the superintendent general of Indian affairs and the Minister of Fisheries have a common interest, and perhaps the remarks I make in respect of this particular item during our discussion of the fisheries estimates will serve to shorten the remarks I might otherwise make during our consideration of the Indian affairs branch. I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to some interesting comments which appear in a book entitled "The Indians of British Columbia" by Hawthorn, Belshaw and Jamieson, and which I believe is still considered to be a basic work as far as a survey of the situation in respect of Indians in that province is concerned. This information is now old but it was produced at the instigation of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in an attempt to provide a social and economic survey of the Indians of British Columbia. Perhaps I might refer briefly to chapter 10 which is entitled, "The fishing industry", the first paragraph of which states:

The fishing industry is by far the most important field of employment and livelihood for Indians in British Columbia. As shown in table III in chapter 7, more than 2,000 Indians derive their main source of livelihood from various branches of fishing itself, and another 1,000 or more, the vast majority of whom are women, from fish canning or processing.
The chapter goes on to describe the historic pattern of the industry as it has affected the livelihood of the Indian people. I think it is apparent that since the incursion of the white man into what was originally the basic means of livelihood of the native people of British Columbia the pattern has had its ups and downs with, unfortunately, a good many more downs than ups. I think it emerges rather clearly from a study of this chapter that the developments taking place at the time this work was produced and which have been proceeding at an accelerated pace since 1958 have tended to remove more and more Indian people from their proper status within this industry. On page 112 there is this reference to recent developments:
There have been a number of other Important developments in the fishing industry of British Columbia in recent years. In different branches of the fishing industry and in different areas of the coast they present a somewhat confusing picture, in which it is difficult to assess accurately the present and future status of Indians in fishing and canning employment.
Then it goes on to refer to the rapid technological changes that have been taking place both in the fishery and processing sections of the industry. If the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will refresh their minds with the outline contained in this chapter of the book it will become clear to them that one of the problems the Indian people have been and are faced with is that they have been pushed into a poorer and poorer economic position relatively speaking, and that by and large the relative efficiency of the type of fishing gear they have been able to acquire and use has declined in relation to the kind of gear used by the whites and by the Canadians of Japanese ancestry. This is presenting a most serious problem.
The book makes clear that many of the Indian people today are in the position of being marginal fishermen. At the conclusion of the chapter on the fishing industry as it affects the Indians there is an attempt to make some recommendations. The authors suggest that in some respects it may perhaps be better if many of the Indian people would move into other industries. I should like to refer to the last paragraph in this chapter

because I think it has particular point in view of what has happened since the book was written. On page 123 the authors say:
One saving feature in this situation is that those coast bands who seem to face the greatest threat of mass displacement from fishing, particularly in the Skeena and Nass areas and on the west coast of Vancouver island, live in heavily timbered areas in which intensive logging and lumber processing operations are likely to be under way in the fairly near future. The whole problem, however, requires further surveys and investigation, particularly of the employment and income potentials of timber resources accessible to Indian bands in each major district.
I realize that my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena, is much more familiar with the Skeena and Nass areas than I am, but with respect to the west coast of Vancouver island, where many of the fishermen have been pushed into a very marginal position, the fact of the matter is that in spite of the statement that there are large timber resources on the west coast of the island, which is correct, the economic opportunities in that field which have opened up to the Indian people since this book was written in 1958 have been very limited indeed. One reason for this has been the kind of policies that have been adopted at the provincial level in respect of allocating the forest resources for harvesting.
I should like to refer to one particular community of Indians, Ahousat, whose reserve is located on the seashore in the midst of a tremendous area of forest resources. In spite of a number of years of intensive effort on the part of the member of the provincial legislature for Alberni to have steps taken leading to the development of employment opportunities in the logging industry for the people of Ahousat, the fact is that most of them at the present time are in a very marginal economic position and are living under conditions which I am sure the minister, if he is aware of them, would have to agree are completely disgraceful. A forest management licence for the whole area has been granted to one major forest products concern. Some of us have attempted to argue that an economic log producing unit should be established to provide employment opportunities for these people, but so far no such steps have been taken.
The fact remains that the Ahousats, like most of the people on the west coast of Vancouver island, are historically a fishing people and would like to be able to continue to fish. However, because of the change brought about by the removal from the west coast of Vancouver island of the many fish canning
Supply-Fisheries
and processing plants which existed there, because of the fact that technological change has resulted in fishermen from other areas being able to range far and wide into areas where the Indian fishermen cannot go in their small boats, because of the fact that the plenitude of fish close inshore has dropped to the point where they find it difficult to fish in a way which will return an income above marginal level, these people in fact are really not in the fishing industry in the way that they were. In days gone by they were known far and wide for their skill in fishing. The Ahousat people at one time played a large part in whaling and sealing. They have a long tradition in the fishery and it is their most natural occupation.
The Minister of Fisheries will recall that not long ago the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration announced the beginning of a community development program for the Indian people. I suggest that here is an area where there should be the closest co-operation between the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Department of Fisheries so that a realistic program of community development can be initiated along the west coast of Vancouver island. I suggest that one thing that is needed is a program which will enable the Indian people in these smaller west coast communities, of which I have used Ahousat as an example, to compete efficiently in the fishery.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration knows that there are certain funds available to his department to assist the Indian people in obtaining fishing vessels and gear; but these funds are completely inadequate, and the arrangements under which they can be had are completely unrealistic so far as putting the fisherman in a competitive position with other fishermen is concerned. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that the role his department should play in this field is to see that these people are being treated fairly and receive the same amount of attention in respect of credit arrangements for modern fishing vessels and gear as any other citizen in any other part of Canada. This is simply not the case at the present time.
So, Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to express, as briefly as I can, what I feel is a very important aspect of the fishing industry and a very important concern so far as the superintendent general of Indian affairs is concerned, at a time when both ministers happen to be in the house.

Supply-Fisheries
I hope both ministers will take note of this situation and work together to do something about it.

Before we proceed to pass item 1, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a series of questions relating to expenditures in the past year for a variety of items and programs, with a division of those expenditures as between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. I should like to start with the Newfoundland bait service. I would assume from the name of it that the moneys spent are spent mainly on the Atlantic coast and that none of this money is available for the Pacific coast because Newfoundland does not extend that far, even though I am sure some Newfoundlanders think it does or would like it to. Can the minister tell me with respect to the Newfoundland bait service the amount of money that has been spent during the past year?

If the hon. member wants an immediate answer, I would say that last year we spent for the Newfoundland bait service-this includes the construction of the new Arctica-$1,148,000. Normally, the total expenditure for a year is about $400,000. This amount is just for Newfoundland because it is provided under an agreement under the terms of confederation.
Can the minister tell me also with respect to the operations under the Fisheries Prices Support Act, what have been the expenditures on the Pacific coast and the expenditures on the Atlantic coast?

Under the prices support board, as I mentioned in my earlier remarks, the administration expenditures this year have been moderate, namely, $62,866. There was no direct support given last year. This year we expect to have about $25,000, I believe, for the Magdalen islands, and about $60,000 was set aside for support for the sauger fishery in the prairies. This is as a result of a lack of markets for smoked fish.
Would this be the first year of operation for the Fisheries Prices Support Act in the prairies?
No, it has been effective in that area in the past.
There have been no expenditures under this act on the Pacific coast?
Not last year.

Can the minister indicate to me the amount of money that has been

expended by way of subsidy under the so-called fishing vessel construction program, again dividing it as between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts?
As the hon. member knows, the subsidy program is only applicable to the Atlantic coast. The amount spent last year was approximately $500,000.

Can the minister tell me the expenditure in connection with the salt subsidy program, and whether or not that is exclusively expended on the Atlantic coast, or whether the Pacific coast is involved as well?
The salt subsidy program also applies to the Atlantic coast. The total expenditures last year were slightly over $600,000.

There is an item in the estimates for grants to the Nova Scotia fisheries exhibit at Lunenburg, which is exclusively a matter for the Atlantic coast, of $3,000. I wonder if the minister can give me a breakdown of the grants to Canadian universities as between universities on the Atlantic coast and universities on the Pacific coast?

The grants to universities are as follows: St. Francis Xavier, $51,700; the social economics service, Ste Anne de la Poca-tiere, $27,100; University of British Columbia, $11,200; Memorial University, St. John's Newfoundland, $30,000.

There is an item referred to in the estimates as development and demonstration of fishing vessels and gear. I wonder if the minister could tell me the expenditures under that item, again divided as between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts?

This answer, Mr. Chairman, would require detailed study if we were to separate the amounts. The total expenditure amounted to $195,000, and I would say that a large proportion of this was spent on the east coast although some demonstrations have taken place in the great lakes area and in British Columbia.

There is another item following that with regard to development and demonstration facilities for processing, packaging, storing and transportation. I assume that perhaps I will get a similar answer from the minister, that it would be difficult to break down the expenditures.
Yes, it would be difficult unless we had notice that a detailed study was required.
Could I at this stage ask the minister it he would be kind enough to make that study and communicate by letter whatever information is available?
I will be pleased to do that.
Will the minister communicate also with respect to the amount of money paid for the destruction of harbour and grey seals, divided as between the east and west coasts?

I do not have the exact figures, but I can tell the hon. member that the larger proportion if this expenditure was on the west coast. In fact we had a shortage of funds there about a month ago, because all our appropriation was expended.
Am I correct in assuming that the bait freezing subsidy is also limited to the Atlantic coast or is the Pacific coast involved as well?

The bait freezing subsidy applies to the Atlantic coast, and the main reason is that this is the area where there is a requirement for bait because of the type of fishing which is practised there. The total expenditures last year were $22,670.

Mr. Chairman, these are helpful figures and it is helpful information. What I was trying to do, perhaps, was to substantiate the argument I have put forward in various speeches, namely that there appears to be an imbalance between the expenditures by the Department of Fisheries on the Atlantic coast as compared with the Pacific coast. I hope no one will misinterpret what I have said. I am not in any way decrying the fact that expenditures are made and services are provided by way of subventions for salt, subsidies for the purchase of squid for bait, for fishing vessel construction, and so on. I do not know the Atlantic coast fisheries, but I am quite sure there are a lot of grants for the Atlantic coast and the maritime province of Newfoundland that are quite well justified, and necessary to preserve the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast. However, there appears to me to be an inordinately large amount of preference given to Atlantic coast fisheries by the department, as compared with that provided for the Pacific coast fisheries.
I know that fishermen at home in B.C. on the west coast make inquiries from time to time about various assistance programs. They want to know about this bait freezing subsidy. They do not freeze bait on the Pacific coast
Supply-Fisheries
but they could get some assistance in this way. We do not salt fish on the west coast, but the fishermen there ask, especially in difficult years when prices are low, such as last year and the year before, why there cannot be some provision made to assist or subsidize some section of the industry on the west coast, so that the fishermen there could get a little better opportunity to make a more decent income than they do now. There is this concern about the heavy weighting of consideration for the Atlantic coast fisheries vis-a-vis those on the Pacific coast.
I was waiting for the minister to make some comment about a telegram which I hope has been forwarded to him, dealing with this very question. It involves the fishing vessel subsidy and the order in council which sets out that this is exclusively for the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. The Pacific coast is specifically excluded from the operations of the fishing vessel subsidy, and on August 28 Mr. Guy Williams, who is president of the native brotherhood of B.C., sent a telegram to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration which I think I should read. It said:
Forward to Minister of Fisheries, Hon. H. J. Robichaud. Request you act on behalf of native fishermen in B.C. to be included in extension of fishing vessel assistance regulations as in five provinces. Minimum length of 35 foot boats ideal for combination gillnet-troller and longline operation.
No less than 100 fishermen need immediate assistance first year. Ninety five per cent of small Indian fishing boats in state of ill repair and not suitable for required mobility of today's operations. Detailed letter at later date on above.
Guy R. Williams
This is an indication of the concern that fishermen have on the west coast. They ask themselves this simple question: Aren't we Canadians too? Why can fishermen on the Atlantic coast, in the maritime provinces and in the province of Quebec, qualify for the 25 per cent or 30 per cent subsidy for the building of fishing boats, when we are excluded from that? This is a very serious question that concerns the people in B.C. For many years there has appeared to be an orientation of the federal government toward the east, toward in some respects-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Very happily.

Have the fishermen on the west coast made serious attempts to take the benefit of the subsidies that go into the

Supply-Fisheries
building of these ships? I hope the hon. member can enlighten me on that because I have tried to get that information over the last 18 months.

The minister has not exhausted himself if he tried for 18 months and has not been successful. Undoubtedly he was one of those who, on June 11 of this year, participated in passing the order in council with respect to the fishing vessel assistance regulations which sets out that these regulations apply only to the province of Nova Scotia through the fishermen's loan board, to the province of New Brunswick through the fishermen's loan board, to the province of Prince Edward Island through the fishermen's loan board, to the province of Newfoundland through the fishermen's loan board, and to the province of Quebec through the minister of industry and commerce.

Would the hon. member answer my question? What representations have been made by the fishermen on the west coast? Plenty have been made on the east coast, but what representations have been made by the west coast fishermen?

Perhaps I may tell my hon. friend this is due to the failure-which I think is a ruddy shame-of his own party, which I understood was to treat Canadians as equals. It may be due to the failure of members of his own party. Not one single member of the Liberal party from B.C. has participated in the discussion so far today or yesterday, on the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. This is a shameful thing.
What sort of representations have been made by them? Isn't the minister himself a member from B.C.? Doesn't he know himself about these things? Where was he when the cabinet passed this discriminatory order in council that discriminates against B.C. fishermen? Was the Postmaster General in on that cabinet meeting? Why didn't he speak up and say something?
What about the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister? What about the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, a home born British Columbian? Isn't he interested in the fishermen of B.C.? Did he not have the intestinal fortitude to speak up and object to this discriminatory order in council when it was passed by the cabinet on June 11 this year?
Perhaps if the Postmaster General searched his own party and his own concern for the welfare of the fishermen at home he would

find the answer, rather than standing up and exhibiting his ignorance, asking me questions about what representations have been made. Here is a telegram that was sent by Guy Williams, president of the native brotherhood of B.C., making reference to this matter and asking for something to be done. What has happened since then? Is anything to be done? Are these people at home to continue to be looked upon as second class citizens, unworthy of equal treatment by this department? This is a very serious question, and perhaps the minister would like to answer me.

So far as expenditures are concerned I realize the hon. member has brought to light some programs provided for the Atlantic coast, but I would like to refer briefly to the Nanaimo station where the research board is spending close to $2 million, to the $210,000 we are spending on the international Pacific halibut commission, to the $295,000 we are spending on the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission. These are only some of our expenditures on the west coast.
So far at the telegram which the hon. member read is concerned, it was only brought to my attention this morning through correspondence with my colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I understand the telegram was supposed to have been sent to me, but we have no record of its having been received at my office, and following a letter I received from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration I asked him to send me a copy of that telegram which, as I say, was brought to my attention this morning.
What are you going to do about it?
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, you do not expect me to take a decision within 24 hours. We are certainly going to study the problem, find out what the situation is and find out what can be done.

It is correct, as shown in the main estimates, that $1,885,000 is to be spent on the biological research station at Nanaimo, $323,000 on the technological research station in Vancouver and $204,000 on the oceanographic group in Nanaimo, making a total of about $2,300,000 or $2,400,000 expenditure on the Pacific coast by the fisheries research board, but the minister has failed to mention that the total amount to be spent by the research board is over $6 million, the bulk of which goes to the Atlantic coast.
And the prairie provinces, and also an additional $250,000 to the Vancouver aquarium.

Item agreed to.
Fisheries management and development-
5. Operation and maintenance including Canada's share of the expenses of the international commissions detailed in the estimates and of the costs of programs and projects shared jointly with the provinces and industry, $12,949,100.

I have listened to the discussion with a great deal of interest and I can assure the minister after listening to the last speaker and the argument he raised about whether or not more money is spent on the east coast fisheries than the west coast fisheries that we in Ontario in the inland fisheries would be tickled to death to accept either one as our allocation in the matter of fisheries.
You should get the Postmaster General to argue for you.

I would bring to the minister's attention the fact that I do not wish to deal in detail with the troubles of management and research into the fishing industry in the great lakes because I am sure the minister and his department are quite familiar with the main problem which has been brought out, namely the matter of pollution in the lakes. Underneath the surface of lake Erie there is a mass of insoluble sludge and slime, no one knows exactly how many feet deep, coming down the Detroit river and rolling out over the bottom of lake Erie, and when the fishermen on the lake drop their nets they become covered with this slime. This makes fishing a terrible job and is causing many fish to die. The lake is becoming a terrible place to fish. It has become so contaminated that bathing beaches are being closed down. They are talking of it as the dead lake and people are asking me whether I realize that lake Erie has now become a dead lake. The boats which go out on the lake and return to shore are covered with an inch or so of this slime all over their bottoms and keels. The condition is getting worse and the fishermen there want to know whether anything can be done, and if anything is being done now.
Commercial fishing in lake Erie is now confined to two main species, smelt and perch. Only a few years ago hundreds of thousands of pounds of other varieties were taken out of the lake. It seems sad that those who fish on lake Erie are within reach of a 24-hour refrigerated truck service which 20220-533
Supply-Fisheries
can supply perhaps 30 million people in Canada and the United States with fish. We have a market for the products of the lakes, which have found a ready favour in both the United States and Canada; but now we are faced with a depletion of the fish in the lake. We have an entire industry geared for production, and we now find the fishermen in most parts running into dire economic straits, abandoning their ships in many instances and looking for other types of work. This is a sorry situation, and these men are asking that something be done right away. They are not concerned with who is responsible, but what they are concerned with is what steps are being taken, when they will be taken, and how effective they will be.
The minister spoke about federal-provincial committees.. The fishermen in the area are sick and tired of approaching over the years provincial governments and federal governments, going back and forth seeking an answer to their problems. They have always received sympathetic consideration and have always felt that the officials they approached have seriously tried to do something about their problems. But somewhere there seems to be a breakdown in communications between the federal and provincial governments, which has meant that the fishermen did not receive the consideration which they felt was necessary. I would ask the minister whether it is his opinion that this federal-provincial committee will now provide the necessary pipe line to enable these fishermen to get the immediate help they so desperately need.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena because our problem is exactly the same as his. We in Ontario want to know why our fishermen cannot get the same sort of insurance on their boats, and the shipbuilding subsidies, which the fishermen in the other five provinces receive. Our fishermen build boats which vary in length from 55 feet to 65 feet and are valued at anywhere from $30,000 to $90,000 each. But they need help with new boats, nets and supplies and they are anxious to know whether any money will be made available to them. Will there be any new legislation so that these fishermen can insure their boats to the degree necessary under the conditions they fish today? Are they going to get the necessary money to provide new equipment and new boats? Is this going to be provided, now that we have a new federal-provincial committee?

Supply-Fisheries
Another matter I wish to mention is one which I am sure the minister is well aware of; it has been brought to his attention on various occasions and representations have been made to him. It is the formation of a co-operative for the fishermen on lake Erie. The fishermen on lake Erie are not only faced with the fact that the fish in the lake are being depleted, but also the price of the fish varies from 1J cents a pound to 18 to 20 cents a pound, depending on the amount of fish on the market at the time. I am sure the minister is aware that one matter which is standing in the way of the formation of a co-operative is the legislation block, which has been brought to his attention. The fishermen have approached the province on the matter and at this point I should like to quote from a letter sent to me by these fishermen. They say, in part:
Accordingly the farm products marketing board of Ontario is of the opinion that the proposed lake Erie fish marketing plan would be of little value until the necessary federal legislation is enacted and is withholding any further action on the request of this association-
I am sure that this was brought to the attention of the minister, and his answer to them on July 27-and I do wish to thank him for the courtesy of his consideration and his proper reply-he pointed out that a new committee was being set up to study this entire program, and that a local member of the association was secretary of the new committee.
According to a newspaper article dated July 20, in Winnipeg the federal-provincial study committee recommended the establishment of a prairie fish exports marketing board, and I am wondering whether there would be the same value in an Ontario board. This newspaper went on to say that the three major fish buyers in Chicago and Detroit could set the price which will be paid for Canadian fish in the United States. I hope that this is why a co-operative is being established-to combat the setting of prices in the United States rather than to further the setting of prices.
They are the problems which I bring to the attention of the minister and I hope he will have the answers that these fishermen need. It is purely a question of economics. The fish seem no longer to be in the lake. What is being done at the London research centre and at other local research centres to see why these fish are being depleted, and what can be done to put them back? What is being done to enact the right legislation in order to make it possible for these fishermen

to form a co-operative if they so desire? What is being done to put our fishermen on the same basis as the fishermen on the east coast, and even those on the west coast, who have more money, subsidies and legislation to enable them to further their business? As I am sure the minister and his departmental officials are well aware, it is simply a matter of pure economics. If the fishermen can make more money they can stay in business. If they cannot make more money the industry is going to fail. Surely we in Ontario especially cannot afford to let this multi-million dollar industry fail without making desperate efforts at the federal level to try to see if it cannot be established on a paying basis.
Mr. Chairman, I should like you to tell me which vote we are on at the moment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Vote No. 5. Shall the vote carry?
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two questions I want to ask the minister on vote No. 5. As the minister is probably quite well aware, the Shell Oil Company has been conducting certain explorations off the west coast of Vancouver island, operating from a base at Ucluelet. In the course of their oil explorations they have been carrying out certain tests which involve the use of explosives, in underwater explosions. A great deal of concern has been expressed from time to time as to the effect of these explosions on the fish population in that area.
I understand that the matter has been under observation by the Department of Fisheries and I wonder whether the minister has available and could give to the committee for the record the fisheries department's knowledge in this regard and just what has happened in respect to the destruction of the fish population.

Mr. Chairman, this operation by the Shell Oil Company on Vancouver island is under close observation of the officials of the department. If at any time we find it affects the fish population, we are prepared to order that the operation stop until we can study the matter further.

Has the department available a detailed report on this matter? I noted in the recent publication of the fisheries association of B.C. certain statistics which they say come from the Department of Fisheries; it was some report of the Department of

Fisheries. I must say that I have not seen that report issued by the department. I was wondering whether the minister has it available and can put these statistics on the record; or if not, can he indicate how that information is officially available from the department?
Mr. Chairman, we have no official report to give. We can certainly prepare a statement to that effect and make it available to the hon. member, and I will do this.

Mr. Chairman,
there are two or three questions that I want to ask the minister-I will try to be brief- regarding the new regulations which he spoke of with regard to seals. I think he said he had discussed the matter with representatives of the S.P.C.A. I believe he has been written to by the Audubon society also, and I presume he has discussed this matter with them. They have expressed keen interest in this matter, and I would like to be assured that these representations are being considered.
Under this item, Mr. Chairman, I would refer to the latest figures we have for revenue from the north Pacific fur seal treaty. These are for the fiscal year 1962-63, which show a revenue of almost half a million dollars. I wonder whether the minister could conveniently give us the revenue, either gross or net, for the last fiscal year, 1964, if that figure is available. Also, is the minister in a position to make a brief statement about the conclusion to which his department has come with regard to the effect that the Mactaquac dam may have on salmon migration in the Saint John river, especially with regard to the effect this dam would be expected to have on the Tobi-que run, and all the runs that migrate above that location on the Saint John river.

Mr. Chairman, I would reply briefly to the questions asked by the hon. member. In so far as our contacts with the S.P.C.A. and the Audubon society are concerned, I cannot confirm at this time whether we have had representations from the Audubon society. I believe we have. We will certainly make an effort to contact them and make them aware of the amendments we have in mind.
The return on investments for seals amounted to $466,989, and the proceeds from the sales were $176,758. In so far as the Mactaquac is concerned, we have made a thorough survey of the project and have come to complete agreement with the province of New 20220-533J
Supply-Fisheries
Brunswick to build in this connection probably one of the most modern and efficient hatcheries in the world. We are combining the knowledge of our scientists and the knowledge of the Swedish scientists in this regard. We can give the assurance that when this project is being proceeded with the salmon population of the Saint John river will be fully protected; in fact, we intend to have enough production from this hatchery to supply not only the Saint John river but other rivers in New Brunswick.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister could supply some answers to the questions I posed a few minutes ago?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I can reply briefly to the points raised by the hon. member. So far as pollution of the lake Erie area is concerned, we are well aware of the situation. It is a very complex problem which affects not only the provincial government and the municipalities but all the industries along the lake shore area. It is also an international problem. The hon. member mentioned the federal-provincial committee, which is studying this matter further. We are also looking into the matter of the co-op marketing plan, which requires legislation as the hon. member says; but it requires provincial legislation. We are now in the course of discussions with the provincial authorities in order to determine what can be done in this sphere, not only for that particular co-op but for a marketing board in regard to the whole production of the inland fisheries.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one question on vote No. 5. There is an item on page 148 which refers to community fishing stages, in the amount of $25,000, compared with $50,000 in the previous fiscal year. I wonder whether the minister could tell us what this item is for. What are community fishing stages, and what is the explanation in regard to the decrease?

Community stages are being built, principally in Newfoundland; in the outposts of that province, in very small areas where there are no facilities, no fishing company to buy the fish and where the fishermen have to process their own fish. We are providing for them what we call a community shed, in which they can store their salted fish until the buyer calls in the fall for their production.

Item agreed to.
.8422

15. Grants, contributions and subsidies in the [DOT]amounts and subject to the terms specified in the sub-vote titles listed in the details of estimates, $1,050,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of delaying these estimates, but I am .anxious under vote 15 to congratulate the provincial government of Newfoundland upon its initiative, its imaginative initiative I might say, in instituting the new fisheries college. This is obviously a very forward looking effort on the part of the provincial government and its beneficial effects will be felt far outside the province of Newfoundland; indeed they will be felt in all Canada.
I would urge the federal government and the Minister of Fisheries to give earnest consideration to assisting this fisheries college in every possible manner. May I also support the hon. members who have spoken, especially those from my own province, and suggested that we spend more money on conservation and research. In that respect I am very happy that the minister said this afternoon that over $1 million more will be spent this year than was spent last year on research. I do not need to . urge the minister to remember the fisheries college; I know he needs reminding only that this is a very worth-while effort, which not only deserves but demands, even commands, our enthusiastic support.
I cannot help at this moment suggesting to the hon. member for Skeena that when he is compiling his statistics on the fishermen of Newfoundland, whom he seems to feel are very well taken care of as compared with the fishermen of British Columbia, he should look up the average wage. He will find it is something like $800 in Newfoundland, v. $4,000 in British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, this is what I was hoping would not happen, that any member from a constituency of one of the Atlantic .provinces would think I was picking on him or the Atlantic fishermen. I had no intention of doing that. I was just pointing out the disparity that exists in respect of federal government assistance on the Atlantic and Pacific cpasts. The hon. member has talked about an average income of a fisherman on the Pacific coast in the amount of $4,000. I wish he would come out and tell some of the gill-net fishermen that their average is $4,000. I am sure he would get wet as a result of being thrown in the ocean.

Item agreed to.

Fisheries research board of Canada-
20. Administration, operation and maintenance including an amount of $75,000 for grants for fisheries research and for scholarships and authority to make recoverable advances of amounts not exceeding in the aggregate the amount of the share of the international great lakes fishery commission of the cost of work on lamprey control and lamprey research, $5,865,000.

Mr. Chairman, if my understanding is correct this item has to do with the granting of money for the operation of the fisheries research board of Canada, and in view of the value of the work done by that board and the appreciation expressed by those of us who have knowledge and experience in this field I certainly think it would be a mistake to pass this item without comment. As far as I am concerned, I think a discussion in depth and in detail in relation to the operations of this board should be referred to the committee on marine and fisheries, as was suggested earlier. I certainly hope that in light of an earlier statement by the minister in relation to next year's estimates, that this is one of the matters we will have an opportunity to examine and discuss in that committee next year.
That is an undertaking, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to raise anything objectionable at this time, and I am not asking you to see the time, but it is now 10.05 and if we are to proceed past the normal hour of adjournment we should do so by unanimous consent, rather than as a result of inadvertence or blindness on the part of anyone.
